name: The Seven Primitive Types
key_idea: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol and null. Everything else is an object. `typeof` names the type, with two surprises: `typeof null` is `"object"`, and a function gives `"function"`.

name: Numbers Are Floating Point
key_idea: Every number is a 64-bit float. Whole numbers are exact up to 2^53 - 1. Fractions such as 0.1 are not, so `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3`.

name: NaN, Infinity and -0
key_idea: Bad maths gives `NaN`, not an error. `NaN` is not equal to itself, so test for it with `Number.isNaN`. Dividing by zero gives `Infinity`. `-0` exists and equals `0`.

name: BigInt
key_idea: A BigInt is a whole number of any size, written with an `n` at the end. It cannot mix with numbers in maths, and its division drops the fraction.

name: Strings Are Immutable
key_idea: A string is a fixed sequence of characters. You can read a character by its index, but no method changes a string: each one returns a new string.

name: Template Literals
key_idea: Backticks make a string that can span lines and hold `${expression}`. The expression is evaluated and converted to a string.

name: null and undefined
key_idea: `undefined` is what JavaScript gives when a value is missing: an unset variable, a missing property, a function with no `return`. `null` is a value you set yourself to say "nothing here".

name: Values and References
key_idea: A primitive is copied when it is assigned. An object is not: the variable holds a reference, so two variables can point at one object. `===` on objects compares identity, not content.

name: Truthy and Falsy
key_idea: Eight values are falsy: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `[]` and `{}`.

name: Converting to a String
key_idea: `String(x)` and template literals convert any value to text. An array joins its items with commas, and a plain object becomes `[object Object]`.

name: Converting to a Number
key_idea: `Number(x)` and unary `+` convert a value to a number. Empty text and `null` give `0`. `undefined` and text that is not a number give `NaN`.

name: parseInt and parseFloat
key_idea: `parseInt` and `parseFloat` read a number from the start of a string and stop at the first character that does not fit. `Number` needs the whole string to be a number.

name: The + Operator
key_idea: `+` joins text if either side is a string. Otherwise it adds numbers. It runs left to right. The other maths operators always convert to numbers.

name: Objects to Primitives
key_idea: To use an object as a primitive, JavaScript calls its `[Symbol.toPrimitive]` method, or else `valueOf` and `toString`. That is why `[] + []` is an empty string.

name: == and ===
key_idea: `===` compares without converting. `==` converts first: `null` equals only `undefined`, and a string or a boolean becomes a number. Use `===`, except for `x == null`, which tests for both empty values.

name: Comparing with < and >
key_idea: `<` and `>` compare two strings letter by letter, so `"10" < "9"`. Any other mix is converted to numbers, and every comparison with `NaN` is false.

name: Three Kinds of Sameness
key_idea: `===` says `NaN` differs from itself and `0` equals `-0`. `Object.is` says the opposite on both. `includes`, `Map` and `Set` use a third rule: `NaN` is the same as `NaN`, and the two zeros are the same.

name: && and || Return a Value
key_idea: `a || b` gives `a` if it is truthy, else `b`. `a && b` gives `a` if it is falsy, else `b`. They return one of their operands, not a boolean, and skip the right side when it is not needed.

name: The ?? Operator
key_idea: `a ?? b` gives `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined`. Unlike `||`, it keeps `0`, `""` and `false`.

name: Optional Chaining
key_idea: `a?.b` gives `undefined` when `a` is `null` or `undefined`, and skips the rest of the chain. It also guards calls, `f?.()`, and indexes, `a?.[i]`.

name: Assignment Is an Expression
key_idea: An assignment gives back the value it assigned, so `a = b = 1` works from right to left. `||=`, `&&=` and `??=` assign only when the left side calls for it.

name: ++ Before and After
key_idea: `++x` adds one and gives the new value. `x++` adds one and gives the old value.

name: Precedence and Associativity
key_idea: Precedence decides which operator binds first, and associativity decides the order among equals. `**` and assignment group from the right. `typeof` and `!` bind tighter than maths.

name: Destructuring Arrays
key_idea: `const [a, b] = list` takes items by position. You can skip items, give defaults for `undefined` ones and collect the rest with `...rest`.

name: Destructuring Objects
key_idea: `const { a, b } = obj` takes properties by name. You can rename with `a: x`, give defaults and reach into nested objects. Destructuring `null` or `undefined` throws.

name: Spread
key_idea: `...` expands an array or an object into a new one, or into the arguments of a call. The copy is one level deep, and a later property wins.

name: Bitwise Operators
key_idea: Bitwise operators treat a number as a 32-bit integer. `&`, `|`, `^` and `~` work bit by bit, and `<<`, `>>` and `>>>` shift the bits.

name: switch
key_idea: `switch` compares with `===` and runs from the matching `case` until a `break`. Without a `break` it falls through into the next case.

name: Loops, break and continue
key_idea: `break` leaves the nearest loop, and `continue` skips to its next round. A label names an outer loop, so `break outer` leaves both.

name: for...of
key_idea: `for (const x of list)` visits the values of an array, a string or any other iterable. Unlike `forEach`, it can `break`, `continue` and `return`.

name: Automatic Semicolons
key_idea: JavaScript adds a missing semicolon at a line break only when the next line cannot continue the statement. `return` followed by a line break returns `undefined`, and a line that starts with `(` or `[` joins the line before it.

name: let and const
key_idea: `let` declares a variable you can reassign. `const` cannot be reassigned, but the object it holds can still change.

name: Block Scope
key_idea: A `let` or `const` variable lives only inside the `{ }` block where it is declared. An inner block can read outer variables, and can shadow one with its own.

name: var
key_idea: `var` ignores blocks: it belongs to the whole function, or to the whole file. It can be declared twice without an error.

name: Hoisting of var
key_idea: A `var` declaration is moved to the top of its function, but its assignment stays where it is. Before that line the variable holds `undefined`.

name: Hoisting of Functions
key_idea: A function declaration is hoisted with its body, so you can call it above the line where it is written. A function expression follows the rules of its variable.

name: The Temporal Dead Zone
key_idea: `let`, `const` and `class` are hoisted too, but not initialised. Reading one before its declaration line throws a `ReferenceError`.

name: Lexical Scope
key_idea: A function looks up a variable where the function was written, then outward, scope by scope. Where the function is called from does not matter.

name: The Global Object
key_idea: `globalThis` is the global object, and its properties can be read as plain names everywhere. In a module, top-level variables stay inside the module: nothing is global unless you put it on `globalThis`.

name: Strict Mode
key_idea: Strict mode turns silent mistakes into errors, such as assigning to a name that was never declared. Modules and classes are always strict.

name: Three Ways to Write a Function
key_idea: A function can be a declaration, an expression or an arrow. Each makes a value you can store, pass and call. A function with no `return` gives `undefined`.

name: Arrow Functions
key_idea: `x => x * 2` returns its expression with no `return`. A body in `{ }` needs `return`, and an object literal needs parentheses: `() => ({ a: 1 })`.

name: Parameters and Defaults
key_idea: A missing argument is `undefined`, and extra ones are ignored. A default value is used only for `undefined`, and it is evaluated again at each call.

name: Rest Parameters and arguments
key_idea: `...args` collects the remaining arguments in a real array. The older `arguments` object holds all of them, is not an array and does not exist in arrow functions.

name: Arguments Are Shared, Not Copied
key_idea: A function gets the same object the caller has. Changing that object inside the function shows outside. Reassigning the parameter does not.

name: Functions as Values
key_idea: A function is a value. You can pass it to another function as a callback, return it from a function, and store it in a variable or an object.

name: Functions Are Objects
key_idea: A function is an object with properties. `name` is its name, `length` counts the parameters before the first default or rest, and you can add properties of your own.

name: The Call Stack
key_idea: Each call is pushed on the call stack and popped when it returns. JavaScript runs one call at a time: the one on top.

name: Recursion
key_idea: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case. Each call waits on the stack, so recursion with no base case overflows it.

name: Closures
key_idea: A function keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished. The function together with those variables is a closure.

name: Closures Hold Variables, Not Values
key_idea: A closure sees the variable itself, not a copy of its value. It reads the latest value, and two closures from the same scope share the variable.

name: Closures in Loops
key_idea: With `let`, each round of a `for` loop gets its own variable, so each closure keeps its own value. With `var`, all the closures share one variable and see its last value.

name: Private State with Closures
key_idea: Variables inside a function cannot be reached from outside. A function that returns other functions gives them private state, and each call makes a new, separate copy.

name: Immediately Invoked Functions
key_idea: `(function () { ... })()` defines a function and calls it at once. It gives code a private scope, which is how modules were built before `import`.

name: this in a Method Call
key_idea: In `obj.method()`, `this` is the object before the dot. `this` is set at each call, not when the function is written.

name: this in a Plain Call
key_idea: A function called without an object gets `undefined` as `this` in strict mode. In old non-strict code it gets the global object.

name: Losing this
key_idea: A method taken off its object is a plain function. Passing `obj.method` as a callback loses `this`. Wrap the call in an arrow function to keep it.

name: call and apply
key_idea: `fn.call(obj, a, b)` calls `fn` with `this` set to `obj`. `fn.apply(obj, [a, b])` does the same with the arguments in an array.

name: bind
key_idea: `fn.bind(obj)` returns a new function whose `this` is always `obj`. It can fix leading arguments too. A bound function cannot be bound again to another object.

name: this in Arrow Functions
key_idea: An arrow function has no `this` of its own. It uses the `this` of the code around it, and `call`, `apply` and `bind` cannot change it.

name: Wrapping Functions
key_idea: A wrapper takes a function and returns a new one that adds behaviour. To stay invisible, it passes `this` and every argument on with `fn.apply(this, args)`.

name: Method Chaining
key_idea: A method that ends with `return this` gives back its object, so calls can be chained: `calc.add(2).multiply(3)`.

name: Object Literals
key_idea: An object maps keys to values. A key is a string or a symbol, and a number key becomes a string. Shorthand, computed keys `[expr]` and method syntax shorten a literal.

name: Reading Properties
key_idea: `obj.key` reads a fixed name, and `obj[expr]` reads a computed one. A missing property gives `undefined`, but reading a property of `undefined` throws a `TypeError`.

name: Does a Property Exist?
key_idea: `"key" in obj` and `Object.hasOwn(obj, "key")` test for a key, even when its value is `undefined`. `delete obj.key` removes the property.

name: Property Order
key_idea: Keys that look like whole numbers come first, in rising order. Then come the other string keys in the order they were added, then symbols.

name: Looping over an Object
key_idea: `Object.keys`, `Object.values` and `Object.entries` give an object's own keys, values and pairs as arrays. `Object.fromEntries` builds an object back from pairs.

name: Shallow Copies
key_idea: `{ ...obj }` and `Object.assign` copy one level. Nested objects are not copied: the copy and the original share them.

name: Updating without Mutating
key_idea: To change nested data without mutating it, copy every level on the path to the change and reuse the rest.

name: Deep Copies
key_idea: `structuredClone` copies a value at every level and handles dates, maps, sets and cycles. It cannot copy functions. A JSON round trip loses more.

name: Getters and Setters
key_idea: `get name()` runs a function when the property is read, and `set name(v)` runs one when it is assigned. From outside they look like a plain property.

name: Property Descriptors
key_idea: Each property has three flags: `writable`, `enumerable` and `configurable`. `Object.defineProperty` sets them, and a flag you leave out is `false`.

name: Freezing Objects
key_idea: `Object.freeze` stops every change to an object's own properties. `Object.seal` only stops adding and removing them. Both are shallow: nested objects stay open.

name: Symbols
key_idea: A symbol is a unique value, made to be used as a property key. Symbol keys never clash with other keys, and `Object.keys`, `for...in` and JSON skip them.

name: JSON
key_idea: `JSON.stringify` turns a value into text. It drops `undefined`, functions and symbols, and turns `NaN` into `null`. `JSON.parse` reads the text back. A replacer, a reviver and `toJSON` customise them.

name: Garbage Collection
key_idea: An object stays in memory while it can be reached from a root: a global, a variable of a running function, or a closure. When nothing reaches it, it is collected.

name: The Prototype Chain
key_idea: Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype. Reading a missing property looks in the prototype, then in its prototype, up to `null`.

name: Writing Does Not Climb the Chain
key_idea: Assigning a property creates it on the object itself and never changes the prototype. In an inherited method, `this` is still the object the call started on.

name: Own and Inherited Properties
key_idea: `Object.keys` and `Object.hasOwn` see only own properties. `in` and `for...in` also see inherited ones.

name: Constructor Functions and new
key_idea: `new F()` makes an object, links it to `F.prototype`, runs `F` with `this` set to it, and returns it. If `F` returns an object, that object is returned instead.

name: The prototype Property
key_idea: Every function has a `prototype` object. Objects made with `new F()` get it as their prototype, so methods put on it are shared by all of them. Its `constructor` points back at `F`.

name: instanceof
key_idea: `obj instanceof F` is true when `F.prototype` is somewhere on the prototype chain of `obj`. It does not look at which function made the object.

name: Built-in Prototypes
key_idea: Array methods live on `Array.prototype`, and every chain ends at `Object.prototype`. A primitive gets a temporary wrapper object for each method call, which is why `"a".toUpperCase()` works.

name: Objects without a Prototype
key_idea: `Object.create(null)` makes an object with no prototype, so it holds only the keys you add. `Object.setPrototypeOf` changes an object's prototype.

name: Inheritance before class
key_idea: To make `Child` extend `Parent` without `class`, link `Child.prototype` to `Parent.prototype` with `Object.create`, and call `Parent.call(this)` in the child constructor.

name: The Four Rules of this
key_idea: `this` comes from how a function is called: with `new`, with `call`, `apply` or `bind`, as a method, or plainly. `new` beats `bind`, and `bind` beats a method call.

name: Detecting a Type
key_idea: `typeof` tells primitives apart. `Array.isArray` finds arrays, `instanceof` checks the prototype chain, and `Object.prototype.toString.call(x)` names any built-in type.

name: Classes
key_idea: A class is a constructor function with a clearer syntax: its methods go on `prototype`. It must be called with `new`, is not hoisted and always runs in strict mode.

name: Class Fields
key_idea: A field such as `count = 0` creates an own property on each instance before the constructor body runs. A field that holds an arrow function keeps `this` bound to the instance.

name: Static Members
key_idea: A `static` method or field belongs to the class itself, not to its instances. Inside a static method, `this` is the class.

name: Private Members
key_idea: A name that starts with `#` is private: only code inside the class body can use it. `#x in obj` tests whether an object has it.

name: Getters and Setters in Classes
key_idea: `get` and `set` in a class define an accessor on the prototype. Every instance shares it, and it is not an own property.

name: extends
key_idea: `class B extends A` links `B.prototype` to `A.prototype`, so instances inherit methods. It also links `B` to `A`, so static members are inherited too.

name: super
key_idea: A derived constructor must call `super()` before it uses `this`. `super.method()` calls the parent's version of a method.

name: Overriding Methods
key_idea: A method in a subclass replaces the parent's method of the same name, even when the parent's own code calls it. The parent's constructor runs before the child's fields exist.

name: Extending Built-ins
key_idea: A class can extend `Array`, `Map` or `Error`. Methods such as `map` and `filter` then return instances of the subclass.

name: Mixins
key_idea: A class can extend only one class. A mixin adds methods from another source: copy them onto the prototype, or write a function that takes a class and returns a subclass.

name: throw, try and catch
key_idea: `throw` stops the running code and climbs the call stack until a `catch` takes the error. Code after the `throw`, in every function on the way up, does not run.

name: finally
key_idea: A `finally` block runs whether the `try` finished, threw or returned. A `return` inside `finally` replaces the result of the `try`.

name: Built-in Errors
key_idea: An error object has a `name`, a `message` and a `stack`. JavaScript throws a `TypeError` for a wrong kind of value, a `ReferenceError` for an unknown name and a `RangeError` for a value out of range.

name: Custom Errors
key_idea: Extend `Error` to make your own error class, and test for it with `instanceof`. Pass `{ cause }` to keep the original error when you wrap one.

name: using and Symbol.dispose
key_idea: `using x = resource` calls `resource[Symbol.dispose]()` when the block ends, even if it throws. Several resources are disposed in reverse order.

name: Arrays and length
key_idea: An array is an object with numbered keys and a `length`. `length` is the highest index plus one, and setting it cuts or extends the array. `at(-1)` reads from the end.

name: Holes in Arrays
key_idea: An array can have holes: indexes with no property at all. A hole reads as `undefined`, but `forEach` and `map` skip it. `Array(3)` makes three holes.

name: Methods That Change the Array
key_idea: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `reverse`, `sort` and `fill` change the array itself. Know what each returns: `push` gives the new length, and `splice` gives the removed items.

name: Methods That Return a New Array
key_idea: `slice`, `concat`, `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with` leave the array as it is and return a new one.

name: map and filter
key_idea: `map` returns a new array with the callback's result for each item. `filter` keeps the items whose callback returns a truthy value. The callback gets the item, its index and the array.

name: reduce
key_idea: `reduce` folds an array into one value. The callback gets the value so far and the next item, and returns the new value. Always pass a start value.

name: Searching an Array
key_idea: `find` and `findIndex` search with a callback. `includes` and `indexOf` search for a value, and only `includes` finds `NaN`. `some` and `every` answer yes or no.

name: Sorting
key_idea: `sort` changes the array and, with no argument, compares the items as strings. Pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers: a negative result puts `a` first.

name: flat and flatMap
key_idea: `flat(depth)` removes levels of nesting. `flatMap` maps each item to an array and flattens the result by one level.

name: Creating Arrays
key_idea: `Array.from({ length: n }, fn)` builds an array from a function. `Array(n).fill(x)` puts the same `x` in every slot, so an object there is shared.

name: Array-likes
key_idea: An array-like has a `length` and numbered keys but no array methods. `Array.from` turns it into a real array.

name: Grouping and Counting
key_idea: `Object.groupBy(items, fn)` sorts items into arrays by the key that `fn` returns. Counting works the same way, with `reduce` or a `Map`.

name: String Methods
key_idea: `slice`, `indexOf`, `includes`, `split`, `replaceAll`, `padStart` and `trim` cover most text work. Each returns a new value and leaves the string as it is.

name: Comparing and Sorting Text
key_idea: `<` compares strings by character code, so every capital letter sorts before every small one. `localeCompare` and `Intl.Collator` sort text the way people expect.

name: Unicode
key_idea: A string is a sequence of 16-bit units, and some characters take two. `length` counts units, while `for...of` and spread walk whole characters.

name: Tagged Templates
key_idea: A tag is a function placed before a template literal. It receives the fixed strings and the values separately, and returns whatever it likes.

name: Patterns and Flags
key_idea: `/pattern/flags` makes a regular expression, and `test` says whether a string matches it. The flag `i` ignores case and `g` finds every match. Escape a special character with a backslash.

name: Character Classes and Anchors
key_idea: `\d`, `\w` and `\s` match a digit, a word character and a space. `[abc]` matches one character of a set, and `[^abc]` one outside it. `^`, `$` and `\b` match a position, not a character.

name: Quantifiers
key_idea: `*`, `+`, `?` and `{n,m}` say how many times to match. They are greedy and take as much as they can. Add `?` to make one lazy.

name: Groups
key_idea: Parentheses group part of a pattern and capture what it matched. `(?<name>...)` names the capture, `(?:...)` groups without capturing, and `\1` matches the same text again.

name: Using a Regex on a String
key_idea: `match` gives the first match with its groups, or every match when the regex has `g`. `matchAll` gives every match with groups. `replace` can use `$1` or a function.

name: lastIndex and the g Flag
key_idea: A regex with `g` or `y` remembers where its last match ended, in `lastIndex`. Calling `test` or `exec` again carries on from there, so the same call can give a different answer.

name: Lookahead and Lookbehind
key_idea: `(?=...)` and `(?<=...)` test what comes after or before a position without making it part of the match. `(?!...)` and `(?<!...)` test that it does not.

name: Regex and Unicode
key_idea: With the `u` or `v` flag a regex works on whole characters, and `\p{...}` matches by Unicode property, such as `\p{L}` for any letter.

name: Map
key_idea: A `Map` holds key and value pairs. Its keys can be any value, objects included. It keeps insertion order and knows its `size`.

name: Set
key_idea: A `Set` holds each value once. Adding a value it already holds does nothing. `[...new Set(list)]` removes duplicates.

name: Set Operations
key_idea: `union`, `intersection`, `difference` and `symmetricDifference` combine two sets into a new one. `isSubsetOf` and `isSupersetOf` compare them.

name: WeakMap and WeakSet
key_idea: A `WeakMap` takes only objects as keys and does not keep them alive. When a key is collected, its entry goes too. It cannot be looped over and has no `size`.

name: Memory Leaks
key_idea: A leak is memory that is still reachable but never used again. The usual causes are a cache that only grows, a timer that is never cleared and a closure that holds a large value.

name: Typed Arrays
key_idea: An `ArrayBuffer` is a block of raw bytes. A typed array such as `Uint8Array` is a view on it with a fixed length and one number type. A value that does not fit wraps around.

name: The Iteration Protocol
key_idea: An iterable has a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method that returns an iterator. An iterator has a `next()` method that returns `{ value, done }`. `for...of`, spread and destructuring all use this.

name: Making an Object Iterable
key_idea: Give an object a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method and it works with `for...of` and spread. Each call should return a new iterator, so the object can be looped over twice.

name: Generators
key_idea: A `function*` returns a generator, which is both an iterator and an iterable. Its body runs only when `next()` is called, and pauses at each `yield`.

name: Talking to a Generator
key_idea: `next(value)` sends a value in: it becomes the result of the paused `yield`. `return()` and `throw()` end the generator early, and `yield*` hands over to another iterable.

name: Lazy Sequences
key_idea: A generator makes values only when asked, so it can describe an endless sequence. Iterator helpers such as `map`, `filter` and `take` are lazy too.

name: The Event Loop
key_idea: JavaScript runs one thing at a time. Code runs until the call stack is empty. Only then does the event loop take the next waiting task and run it.

name: Timers
key_idea: `setTimeout(fn, ms)` queues `fn` as a task after at least `ms` milliseconds. It returns an id that `clearTimeout` cancels. `setInterval` repeats until it is cleared.

name: Asynchronous Callbacks
key_idea: An asynchronous function takes a callback and calls it later, by convention with the error first. A `try` around the call cannot catch an error thrown in the callback, because the `try` has finished by then.

name: Promises
key_idea: A promise stands for a result that comes later. It starts pending, and settles once: fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. The function given to `new Promise` runs at once.

name: then
key_idea: `then` registers a callback for the value and returns a new promise. The callback always runs later, after the current code has finished, even if the promise is already settled.

name: Chaining Promises
key_idea: What a `then` callback returns becomes the value of the next `then`. If it returns a promise, the chain waits for it. Forgetting the `return` breaks the chain.

name: Errors in Promises
key_idea: A rejection skips every `then` until it reaches a `catch`. A `throw` in a callback rejects the next promise. After a `catch` that returns, the chain carries on as fulfilled.

name: Microtasks
key_idea: Promise callbacks wait in the microtask queue. When the current code ends, every microtask runs before the next task, so a `then` callback runs before a `setTimeout` of 0.

name: Promise.resolve and Friends
key_idea: `Promise.resolve(x)` gives a promise fulfilled with `x`, and follows `x` if it is a promise or a thenable. `Promise.reject` gives a rejected one. `Promise.withResolvers` hands out the promise with its `resolve` and `reject`.

name: Promise.all and allSettled
key_idea: `Promise.all` waits for every promise and gives the values in the order of the input. It rejects as soon as one rejects. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all of them and never rejects.

name: Promise.race and any
key_idea: `Promise.race` settles like the first promise to settle. `Promise.any` fulfils with the first one to fulfil, and rejects with an `AggregateError` only when all reject.

name: async Functions
key_idea: An `async` function always returns a promise. What it returns becomes the fulfilled value, and what it throws becomes the rejection.

name: await
key_idea: `await` pauses its function until the promise settles, then gives the value. The rest of the program keeps running. The code after an `await` always runs later, as a microtask.

name: Errors with await
key_idea: `await` throws when its promise rejects, so `try` and `catch` work. A promise that is returned without `await` settles after the `try` block has ended, so its rejection is not caught.

name: One after Another, or Together
key_idea: `await` inside a loop runs the work one after another. To run it together, start every promise first and then `await Promise.all`. `forEach` does not wait for an `async` callback.

name: From Callbacks to Promises
key_idea: To turn a callback function into a promise function, return a `new Promise` and call `resolve` or `reject` inside the callback.

name: Asynchronous Iteration
key_idea: `for await...of` loops over values that arrive later. An `async function*` can `await` and `yield`, and each `next()` returns a promise.

name: What Runs When
key_idea: To find the order of output, run all the synchronous code first, then every microtask, then one task, then the microtasks again.

name: Modules
key_idea: Each file is a module with its own scope. `export` makes a name available, and `import { name }` brings it into another file. Nothing else leaks out.

name: Default Exports and Renaming
key_idea: A module can have one `default` export, which the importer names freely. Named exports can be renamed with `as`, imported together with `* as ns`, and passed on with `export ... from`.

name: Imports Are Live
key_idea: An import is not a copy. It is a read-only view of the exporter's variable, so it shows the latest value. Only the exporting module can assign to it.

name: A Module Runs Once
key_idea: A module's code runs once, the first time it is imported, and every importer shares the result. Imports are hoisted: all the imported modules run before the importing file's own code.

name: import() and Top-level await
key_idea: `import(path)` loads a module when the line runs and returns a promise of its exports. A module can use `await` at the top level, and its importers wait for it.

name: Circular Imports
key_idea: When two modules import each other, one of them runs first and sees the other's exports before they are initialised. A hoisted function works there, and a `const` throws.

name: Well-known Symbols
key_idea: Well-known symbols are hooks into the language. `Symbol.iterator` drives `for...of`, `Symbol.toPrimitive` drives conversion, `Symbol.hasInstance` drives `instanceof`, and `Symbol.toStringTag` names the object.

name: Which Keys Does It See?
key_idea: Each way of listing keys has its own rule. `Object.keys`, spread and JSON see own enumerable string keys. `for...in` adds inherited ones. `Reflect.ownKeys` sees every own key.

name: Reflect
key_idea: `Reflect` holds the basic object operations as functions: `get`, `set`, `has`, `ownKeys`, `apply` and `construct`. They return a result where the operator would throw or fail silently.

name: Proxy
key_idea: A `Proxy` wraps an object and runs your handler on each operation. A `get` trap sees every read and a `set` trap every write. Forward to `Reflect` to keep the normal behaviour.

name: More Proxy Traps
key_idea: `has` handles `in`, `deleteProperty` handles `delete`, `ownKeys` handles key listing, and `apply` and `construct` handle calls. A trap may not lie about a property the target has locked.

name: eval and new Function
key_idea: `eval` runs a string as code in the current scope. `new Function` builds a function from strings that sees only the global scope. Both are slow and unsafe with outside input.

name: Math
key_idea: `Math.floor`, `Math.ceil`, `Math.round` and `Math.trunc` differ on negative numbers and on halves. `Math.max()` of nothing is `-Infinity`.

name: Formatting and Checking Numbers
key_idea: `toFixed` rounds a number and returns a string. `Number.isInteger` and `Number.isSafeInteger` check a number without converting it.

name: Date
key_idea: A `Date` holds one number: the milliseconds since the start of 1970, in UTC. Months count from 0. A value out of range rolls over, so day 0 is the last day of the month before.

name: Temporal
key_idea: `Temporal` replaces `Date`. Its objects never change, months count from 1, and a date, a time, an exact instant and a time zone are separate types.

name: Intl
key_idea: `Intl` formats numbers, dates and lists for a locale. `Intl.NumberFormat` writes currency and percent, and `Intl.PluralRules` picks the right plural form.

name: Memoize
key_idea: A memoized function keeps each result in a cache, keyed by its arguments. A second call with the same arguments returns the cached result without running the function.

name: Curry and Partial Application
key_idea: A curried function takes its arguments one group at a time and runs when it has `fn.length` of them. Partial application fixes some arguments now and takes the rest later.

name: compose and pipe
key_idea: `pipe(f, g)` returns a function that runs `f`, then `g` on its result. `compose` runs them from right to left. Both are one `reduce` over the list of functions.

name: Debounce
key_idea: A debounced function waits until the calls stop. Each call cancels the timer of the call before and starts a new one, so only the last call runs.

name: Throttle
key_idea: A throttled function runs at most once per interval. The first call runs at once, and calls during the wait are dropped or saved for the end.

name: Deep Clone
key_idea: To clone deeply, copy primitives as they are and recurse into arrays and objects. Keep a `WeakMap` from each original to its copy, so a cycle ends instead of looping forever.

name: Deep Equal
key_idea: Two values are deeply equal when they are the same primitive, or have the same kind, the same keys and deeply equal values under each key.

name: Event Emitter
key_idea: An emitter keeps a list of listeners for each event name. `on` adds one, `off` removes it, and `emit` calls each listener with the arguments.

name: Writing map, filter and reduce
key_idea: A polyfill of an array method loops over the indexes, skips the holes and calls the callback with the item, the index and the array.

name: Writing call, apply and bind
key_idea: To call a function with a chosen `this`, store it on the object under a temporary key and call it as a method. `bind` returns a function that does this with saved arguments.

name: Writing new and instanceof
key_idea: `new` is three steps: create an object from `F.prototype`, call `F` on it, and return the object unless `F` returned one. `instanceof` walks the prototype chain looking for `F.prototype`.

name: Writing Promise.all
key_idea: `Promise.all` returns a new promise, stores each result at its own index, counts the results and resolves when the count is complete. It rejects on the first rejection.

name: Timeout and Retry
key_idea: A timeout races the work against a timer that rejects. A retry calls the work again in a loop after each failure, and gives up after a set number of tries.

name: Limiting Concurrency
key_idea: To run many tasks with at most `n` at once, start `n` workers. Each worker takes the next task from a shared index until none are left.

name: Writing a Promise
key_idea: A promise holds a state, a value and a list of waiting callbacks. `then` returns a new promise and queues its callback as a microtask. Resolving with a thenable follows it.
